implementation_notes: The JVM answer is already return-based: declare the constraints as annotations on the request type, obtain a Validator from the Validation factory, and call validate(obj) - it returns a Set<ConstraintViolation<T>> with one entry per failed constraint (empty when valid) and does not throw for validation failures. Spring MVC exposes the same outcome as BindingResult/Errors. Hand-rolled accumulators are only needed when the rules cannot be expressed as constraints or the domain must stay framework-free.
code_sketch:
Validator validator = Validation.buildDefaultValidatorFactory().getValidator();

Set<ConstraintViolation<BookingRequest>> violations =
        validator.validate(request);            // every failure, no throw

List<Problem> problems = violations.stream()
        .map(v -> new Problem(v.getPropertyPath().toString(),
                              v.getMessage(),
                              v.getMessageTemplate()))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
pitfalls: Building a ValidatorFactory per request is wasteful (provider lookup is slow) - build one per application and reuse the thread-safe Validator.
ConstraintViolation.getMessage() is interpolated in the active locale; carry getMessageTemplate() (the code) if the caller must localise.
A class-level constraint can only report the whole object in getPropertyPath(), so field highlighting requires property-level constraints.
Bean Validation deliberately cannot express rules that need services or databases - those need a programmatic notification alongside the declarative one.

variants.name: Hand-written Notification accumulator
variants.implementation_notes: When the rules cannot be expressed as constraints, or the domain must not depend on a validation framework, write the accumulator: a Notification holding a list of errors plus addError and hasErrors, passed into each check or returned by the validation method. Fowler's 2014 example is written in Java and notes that a plain List<String> is a legitimate lightweight form; the class earns its place by making the intent explicit and by giving callers a hasErrors() predicate.
pitfalls: A mutable accumulator shared between threads or reused between requests leaks errors; create one per validation call.
Free-form strings lose the field mapping - carry an error code as Fowler recommends when the presentation must highlight fields.
A check(Notification) method whose only effect is mutating its argument hides the dependency; make the notification an explicit parameter named as such.
